passages.t: Silence, and the prayers of the saints
passages.happening:
The Lamb opens the last seal. John expects, perhaps, a new disaster. Instead there is quiet: “When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (verse 1).

He sees seven angels who stand before God, and “they were given seven trumpets” (verse 2).

Then another angel with a golden censer, a pan for burning incense, comes and stands at the altar. “He was given much incense to offer, along with the prayers of all the saints, on the golden altar before the throne. And the smoke of the incense, together with the prayers of the saints, rose up before God from the hand of the angel” (verses 3-4).

“Then the angel took the censer, filled it with fire from the altar, and hurled it to the earth; and there were peals of thunder, and rumblings, and flashes of lightning, and an earthquake” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 4 to 7 were loud with worship. Now heaven is silent. The Greek word, sigē, comes only twice in the New Testament. Readers take the silence in more than one way: as awe before judgment, as a pause so that the prayers of God's people can be heard, or as the hush before God acts. Each fits the prophets' call to be silent before the LORD.

Then the prayers. In chapter 5 the prayers of the saints were kept in golden bowls. In chapter 6 the martyrs cried, ‘How long?’ Here those prayers rise before God with the incense from the golden altar. In the temple, a priest burned incense at that altar every morning and evening, while the people prayed outside. Now an angel does it in heaven.

And then the answer comes back down. The same censer is filled with fire from the altar and thrown to the earth. Thunder, lightning and an earthquake follow, as at Sinai and around the throne in chapter 4. The seven trumpets that follow are God's answer to his people's prayers.

That is a striking thing to tell small, struggling churches. The prayers of ordinary believers, which seem to change nothing, are shown here as part of how God acts in the world. Christians hold that such prayer reaches God because of Christ, who ‘always lives to intercede’ for those who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25).
passages.ot:
The silence is the prophets' silence before God. “Be silent in the presence of the Lord GOD, for the Day of the LORD is near” (Zephaniah 1:7). “But the LORD is in His holy temple; let all the earth be silent before Him” (Habakkuk 2:20).

The golden altar of incense stood in the holy place of the tabernacle: “And Aaron is to burn fragrant incense on it every morning when he tends the lamps” (Exodus 30:7).

And the fire thrown to the earth echoes Ezekiel, where a man in linen is told to “Fill your hands with burning coals from among the cherubim and scatter them over the city” (Ezekiel 10:2).
passages.hard:
Do the trumpets come after the seals in time, or do they tell the same story again?

Readers divide here, and the answer shapes how the whole book is read. One view reads the series in order: the seventh seal holds the seven trumpets, and the seventh trumpet will hold the seven bowls, so they follow one another toward the end. Many futurists hold a form of this view. Another view, going back to Victorinus of Pettau, reads the series as retelling: seals, trumpets and bowls cover the same span of time, each with greater force, and each ends at the final judgment (compare 6:12-17, 11:15-19 and 16:17-21). Idealists and many others favour this view, noting that the sixth seal already looks like the end. Some combine the two, and see both progress and overlap. These notes do not choose.

On either view the pattern is the same. Judgments come in measured stages, God's people are kept, and the end is certain.
passages.asks: Ask when you last kept silence before God, without words. Ask whether you pray as though your prayers matter to what God does in the world. And ask what prayers you have given up on that this passage says are still before God.

passages.happening:
“And the seven angels with the seven trumpets prepared to sound them” (verse 6).

The first angel blows his trumpet, and John sees “hail and fire mixed with blood were hurled down upon the earth. A third of the earth was burned up, along with a third of the trees and all the green grass” (verse 7).

The second angel blows, “and something like a great mountain burning with fire was thrown into the sea. A third of the sea turned to blood, a third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed” (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
In Israel trumpets called the people to worship and to war, and the prophets used them to sound the alarm before the day of the LORD. At Jericho, seven priests with seven trumpets went before the ark until the walls fell.

The trumpet plagues are built mostly from the story of the exodus. Hail and fire recall the seventh plague on Egypt. Water turned to blood recalls the first. In Egypt, the plagues came before the rescue of God's people. Revelation uses the same pattern: these judgments fall on a world that serves other gods, and they serve a greater rescue, through the Passover Lamb of chapter 5.

Notice the fraction: a third. It comes again and again in these verses. In the seals, a fourth was struck; here, a third; in the bowls, it will be everything. The judgments are severe, but they are partial. Their purpose includes warning and a call to turn back, as chapter 9 will say (9:20-21).

The sea and its ships were the arteries of the empire's wealth. Some readers hear in the burning mountain an echo of the eruption of Vesuvius, which buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in AD 79 and shook the Roman world. The text does not name it, and not every interpreter sees a link. Jeremiah had already called Babylon a ‘destroying mountain’ that God would turn into a burnt mountain, and some see that background here.

The land, the trees, the sea and its creatures are the world God made and called good. Human idolatry does not stay private. It touches the whole creation, which, Paul says, groans as it waits to be set free.
passages.ot:
The hail and fire are Egypt's seventh plague: “the LORD sent thunder and hail, and lightning struck the earth. So the LORD rained down hail upon the land of Egypt” (Exodus 9:23).

The water turned to blood is the first: “Aaron raised the staff and struck the water of the Nile, and all the water was turned to blood” (Exodus 7:20).

The trumpets of alarm are the prophets': “Blow the ram’s horn in Zion; sound the alarm on My holy mountain” (Joel 2:1). And the burning mountain may echo God's word against Babylon: “Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain, you who devastate the whole earth” (Jeremiah 51:25).
passages.hard:
What do the trumpets describe? Do they refer to real events?

Christians read them in the four ways the book page sets out, and these notes do not choose. Preterists connect them with the disasters of the Jewish war and the Roman world in the first century. Historicists have traditionally matched them with invasions that struck the Roman empire in later centuries. Futurists read them as real judgments in a final period before Christ returns. Idealists read them as pictures of how God's judgment runs through history, calling people to repent.

These notes tie no trumpet to any disaster, war, nation or event of our own day. Such matches have been made many times, and they have come and gone. Nor do these pictures say why any particular place or person suffers a disaster. And nothing here makes anyone's illness or death a sign of God's judgment. When his disciples asked whose sin had caused a man's blindness, Jesus answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3).
passages.asks: Ask what it means that God's judgments are measured, a third and not the whole. Ask how you think about the harm human idolatry does to the created world. And ask whether a disaster in the news makes you think of others as worse sinners than you, and what Jesus said about that (Luke 13:1-5).

passages.t: Wormwood, darkness, and the eagle's woe
passages.happening:
The third angel blows his trumpet, “and a great star burning like a torch fell from heaven and landed on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters turned bitter like wormwood oil, and many people died from the bitter waters” (verses 10-11).

The fourth angel blows, “and a third of the sun and moon and stars were struck. A third of the stars were darkened, a third of the day was without light, and a third of the night as well” (verse 12).

Then John hears a cry from the sky: “And as I observed, I heard an eagle flying overhead, calling in a loud voice, ‘Woe! Woe! Woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the trumpet blasts about to be sounded by the remaining three angels!’” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The first four trumpets strike the four parts of the created world, one after another: the land, the sea, the fresh waters and the lights of the sky.

The star is named Wormwood. Wormwood is a plant with a very bitter taste. The Greek word is apsinthos. The prophets used it as a picture of the bitterness that idolatry and injustice bring. Here the fresh water, which people need to live, turns bitter.

The fourth trumpet darkens a third of the sun, moon and stars. That recalls the ninth plague on Egypt, when darkness covered the land for three days.

Then an eagle cries “Woe!” three times. The first four trumpets fell on the world around people. The last three, called ‘woes’, will fall more directly on people themselves, in chapters 9 to 11. The seals were grouped as four and then three, and so are the trumpets.
passages.ot:
Wormwood is the prophets' picture of bitter judgment: “Behold, I will feed this people wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink” (Jeremiah 9:15). Amos uses it of injustice: “There are those who turn justice into wormwood and cast righteousness to the ground” (Amos 5:7).

The darkness recalls Egypt's ninth plague: “So Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and total darkness covered all the land of Egypt for three days” (Exodus 10:22).
passages.asks: Ask what in your own life has turned justice or truth into something bitter. Ask what the eagle's warning would have meant to churches tempted to make peace with their cities' idols. And ask whether you hear Revelation's warnings as a call to turn back, or only as a threat to others.
